Vishnusharman.description: The narrator and storyteller of the Panchatantra, traditionally credited as the author and teacher of the princes.

Book IV.description: The fourth book or section of the Panchatantra, titled 'Loss of Gains.'

blandishments.description: Flattering or coaxing speech or actions intended to persuade someone gently.

Red-Face.description: A clever monkey who lives in a rose-apple tree and uses his wits to escape the treachery of his friend the crocodile.

Ugly-Mug.description: A crocodile who befriends Red-Face the monkey but is later persuaded by his wife to attempt to kill his friend.

Brahman.description: A member of the priestly caste in Hindu society; here, refers both to an individual who has committed a grave sin and, in plural, to the priestly class known for self-denial.

nectar.description: In Indian and classical literature, refers to a sweet, divine drink or substance, often symbolizing immortality.

lawbook.description: Refers to ancient Hindu texts prescribing rules of conduct, such as the Manusmriti.

expiation.description: The act of making amends or reparation for guilt or wrongdoing.

garlands.description: Decorative wreaths of flowers, commonly used in Indian culture for welcoming guests or during celebrations.

rebirthday.description: A figurative term meaning a new lease on life or a second chance at living, often after escaping danger.

Theodore.description: A frog-king who lives in a well and seeks revenge on his relatives by enlisting the help of a black snake named Handsome.

Handsome.description: A black snake who is persuaded by Theodore to enter the well and eat Theodore's relatives.

Theodosius.description: The son of Theodore, who is eventually eaten by Handsome.

Flop-Ear.description: A character mentioned by the monkey as an example of someone who perished by entering danger.

the lizard.description: A lizard who lives in the well and is asked by Handsome to find Theodore and deliver a message.

cistern.description: A tank for storing water, often used in Indian and ancient contexts.

tank.description: A large artificial pool or reservoir for water, commonly found in India.

proverb.description: A short, well-known saying that expresses a general truth or piece of advice.

carpet-slippery.description: A phrase indicating a life of ease or comfort, often used in older English.

subaqueous.description: Existing, formed, or taking place underwater.

rascally.description: Mischievous or dishonest, often used in older English.

hapless.description: Unfortunate or unlucky, used in archaic or literary English.

Fierce-Mane.description: A male lion living in the forest, husband to the lioness and father to the twins, who adopts a jackal cub.

drudge.description: A person or animal who does hard, menial, or dull work.

laundryman.description: A person whose occupation is washing and ironing clothes, often using animals like donkeys for transport.

fodder.description: Food, especially dried hay or straw, for cattle and other livestock.

monks.description: Religious ascetics who renounce worldly life, often referenced in Indian traditions.

frowsy.description: Having a musty or stale appearance; unkempt, often used in older English.

irrevocate.description: An archaic form of 'irrevocable,' meaning unable to be changed or reversed.

prayers.description: Religious invocations or rituals, often performed after bathing in Indian tradition.

potter.description: A man who works with clay and becomes known as Fight-Firm after the king misinterprets a scar on his forehead as a battle wound.

king.description: The ruler of the country where the potter becomes a life-guard; he misinterprets the potter's scar as a battle wound.

princes.description: The sons or noblemen of the king's court who become jealous of the favor shown to the potter.

Your Majesty.description: A formal address used for a king or queen, indicating respect and royal status.

cicatrized.description: Healed by the formation of scar tissue.

potsherd.description: A broken piece of ceramic material, especially from a pot.

cicatrice.description: A scar left by the formation of new tissue over a healing wound.

accountered.description: Equipped or outfitted, especially in reference to soldiers or animals for battle.

caparisoned.description: Dressed in rich decorative coverings, especially referring to horses.

adroitness.description: Skill or cleverness in using the hands or mind.

cuffing.description: A blow or slap, usually with the open hand.

lioness.description: The wife of the lion, mother to the twins, and foster mother to the jackal cub.

twins.description: The two lion cubs born to the lion and lioness, raised with the jackal cub.

elephant.description: A wild elephant who enters the forest, considered an enemy by the lion cubs.

Scripture.description: A reference to sacred or religious texts, likely alluding to Hindu scriptures.

death-god.description: A reference to Yama, the Hindu god of death, symbolizing fate or destiny.

hermit.description: A person living in solitude, often for religious reasons; here, refers to someone who should not be harmed.

clergyman.description: A member of the religious clergy; used in the proverb to indicate someone who should not be harmed.

blighter.description: An archaic English term for a contemptible or unlucky person.

routed.description: Defeated and driven away in disorder.

blossom-lip.description: A poetic phrase describing the jackal's lips, suggesting youth or beauty.

decamp.description: To depart suddenly or secretly, especially to avoid trouble.

absconded.description: Left hurriedly and secretly, typically to avoid detection or arrest.

anecdote.description: A short, amusing or interesting story about a real incident or person.

cripple.description: A disabled man with a heavenly singing voice, whom the Brahman's wife falls in love with and marries.

policemen.description: City officials who discover the cripple in a basket and bring him before the king.

holy man.description: A spiritual figure who rescues the Brahman from the well.

ceremony of purification.description: A ritual act intended to cleanse a person spiritually or ritually.

forest-fruits.description: Fruits gathered from the wild forest, often referenced in Indian fables.

invalid.description: A person weakened or disabled by illness or injury.

basket.description: A woven container, often used in Indian stories for carrying people or goods.

weeping and wailing.description: Crying loudly and showing great distress.

shorn.description: Cut or shaved off, often used in reference to hair or wool.

Joy.description: A king, lord of the sea-girdled earth, renowned for his power and manliness.

Splendor.description: The secretary of King Joy, learned in all scientific text-books, who faces a lovers’ quarrel with his wife.

sea-girdled.description: Surrounded by the sea; often used in ancient texts to describe the earth.

diadems.description: Jeweled crowns or headbands worn as symbols of sovereignty.

footstool.description: A low stool for resting the feet, here symbolizing the subjugation of princes.

henpecked.description: A term describing a man dominated by his wife.

grackle.description: A type of bird, referenced in the proverb.

scot-free.description: Without suffering any punishment or harm.

ass.description: An archaic term for a donkey.

Clean-Cloth.description: A laundryman who owns a single donkey and devises a plan to disguise it in a tiger-skin.

tiger-skin.description: The hide of a tiger, used by Clean-Cloth to disguise his donkey.

barley.description: A type of grain that the disguised donkey eats in the fields.

bray.description: The loud, harsh cry of a donkey.

leading-strings.description: A phrase meaning under the control or guidance of someone else, often used to describe someone dominated by another.

dunderhead.description: An old-fashioned insult meaning a stupid or slow-witted person.

farmer.description: An old man whose wife is discontented and ultimately betrayed by her.

wife.description: The discontented wife of an old farmer who conspires with a rogue to steal her husband's money and seek other lovers.

rogue.description: A thief who deceives the farmer's wife, steals her money and garments, and abandons her.

she-jackal.description: A female jackal who loses both her meat and a fish, and exchanges words with the farmer's wife.

vulture.description: A bird that swoops down and steals the meat from the she-jackal.

fish.description: A fish that is stranded on the bank but escapes back into the river.

rose-apple tree.description: A tropical fruit tree native to South and Southeast Asia, known for its fragrant fruit; it is the specific tree where the monkey resides.

league.description: An old unit of distance, approximately three miles.

rendezvous.description: A meeting place, especially one arranged beforehand.

conciliation.description: The action of stopping someone from being angry; placation.

intrigue.description: The use of secret planning or plotting, often to achieve an objective.

bribery.description: Offering something, often money, to persuade someone to act in one's favor.

sparrow.description: A bird who, along with his wife, built a nest on a tree branch; one of the main characters in this fable.

hen-sparrow.description: The sparrow's wife, known for her outspoken and 'pert' nature; she offers advice to the monkey.

February.description: A month in the Gregorian calendar, referenced here to indicate the time of the story.

heaven.description: A spiritual or divine realm, often referenced in Indian and other religious traditions.

paltry.description: Insignificant or of little value; used here to belittle the hen-sparrow.

plover.description: A type of wading bird, referenced in a proverb.

slut.description: An archaic insult, used here as a term of abuse.

wench.description: An archaic term for a woman, often used insultingly.

obeisance.description: A gesture of respect or submission, such as a bow.

flunkeys.description: Servants or people of low status who are obsequious to those in power.

saintlihood.description: The state or quality of being saintly or virtuous.

recompensing.description: Repaying or compensating, especially in the context of returning good or evil.

Supersmart.description: A clever jackal raised by the lion and lioness as their third son; he devises schemes to eat an elephant and outwits other predators.

tiger.description: A fearful animal who is tricked by Supersmart into leaving the elephant carcass.

leopard.description: A hungry leopard with strong teeth who is persuaded by the jackal to cut open an elephant hide.

second jackal.description: Another jackal who challenges Supersmart for the elephant meat but is driven away.

cudgel-bearer.description: One who carries a cudgel (a short, thick stick used as a weapon), here meaning a guard or servant.

deign.description: To do something considered beneath one's dignity; to condescend.

leavings.description: Remnants or leftovers, especially of food.

self-denial.description: The act of restraining oneself from indulging in desires, often for religious reasons.

fickle.description: Likely to change frequently, especially in loyalty or affection.

ruffian.description: A desperate intruder who forces his way into the crocodile's home and is ultimately defeated.

bill of fare.description: An old-fashioned term for a menu or selection of food.

sobriety.description: Seriousness or moderation, here implying self-control or restraint.
